About this manual

What PTXprint is

PTXprint is a program that makes print-ready PDF files of Scripture. It takes the text from a Paratext project and lays it out on pages: with columns, headings, chapter and verse numbers, footnotes, cross-references, pictures, headers and footers. You can use the PDF for checking and proofreading, or send it to a printer to make a book.

Behind the scenes, PTXprint uses a typesetting program called XeTeX. XeTeX does the work of placing every letter and line on the page. You never need to use XeTeX yourself. You make all your choices in the PTXprint window, and PTXprint tells XeTeX what to do.

PTXprint never changes your Paratext text. It reads the text, makes a temporary copy, and typesets that copy. To correct the words of the text, use Paratext.

Who this manual is for

This manual is for everyone who uses the PTXprint window: translators, typesetters, project leaders and support staff. You do not need to know anything about typesetting or computers to use it.

  • Every instruction in this manual can be done in the PTXprint window. You never need to edit files by hand or type commands.
  • Some sections are marked advanced. They explain how to type special codes in the few places where PTXprint gives you a text box for them (for example the front matter). You can skip these sections until you need them.
  • Technical words are explained the first time they appear in a chapter. They are also listed in the Glossary of terms at the end of the manual.

How this manual is organised

The manual starts with two general chapters. Then there is one chapter for each tab of the PTXprint window, in the same order as the tabs. After that come chapters about the PDF Preview window, importing settings and getting help. The manual ends with step-by-step tasks, solutions to problems, and a glossary.

Most tab chapters have the same parts:

  • What this tab is for – when you would use the tab.
  • One section for each area of the tab, using the names you see on the screen.
  • Common tasks – numbered steps for the things people do most often.
  • Common problems – what you see, why it happens, and what to change.

How to read a settings-reference entry

At the end of each tab chapter, the Settings reference lists every setting (check box, list, number box, button and so on) in that part of PTXprint. Each entry starts with the name of the setting as you see it on the screen. Then it gives some or all of these facts:

  • Where – the path to the setting: the tab, then the area or sub-tab. For example: Layout tab › Page Setup.
  • Type – what kind of control it is, for example a check box, a drop-down list, a number box or a button. For a check box, it also says if it is ticked or not ticked by default.
  • Description – a short name for the setting, when the label on the screen does not say enough.
  • Next to the label – the label that is beside the control on the screen, when this is different from the name of the entry.
  • View level – in which view levels you can see the setting (see below).
  • Values – for a number box: the lowest and highest number you can type, and the default value.
  • Choices – for a drop-down list: the items in the list.
  • Only available when – the setting is greyed out until another setting is turned on.
  • Greyed out when – the setting cannot be used while another setting is turned on.
  • Hidden until – the setting is not shown until another setting is ticked.
  • Tooltip – the help text that PTXprint shows when you hold the mouse over the setting.
  • Explanation – a description in plain words: what the setting does, when to use it, a sensible value, and what to watch out for.

If you cannot find a setting in the window, look first at its View level, then at Only available when and Hidden until.

A short note about view levels

PTXprint has hundreds of settings, but most people need only a few of them. So PTXprint can hide the settings that you do not need. This is called the view level. There are four view levels: Mini, Basic, Default and Full. Mini shows the fewest settings. Full shows every setting.

To change the view level, click the ☰ button at the top-right of the window, point to View Level, and choose a level.

A hidden setting still works. It keeps its value and it still changes the PDF. So if the PDF does not look the way you expect, change to the Full view and check the settings again.

In this manual, a note such as "(Default and Full views)" tells you which view levels show a setting. For more about view levels, see the chapter The main window, menu and view levels.

Getting started with PTXprint

About this chapter

This chapter is for people who are using PTXprint for the first time. It takes you step by step from opening PTXprint to your first PDF. Then it shows you how to change a few common things, and how to keep different sets of settings for different kinds of output.

You do not need to read the rest of the manual before you start. Each step tells you which chapter to read if you want to know more.

In this chapter, "pt" means point. One point is about 0.35 mm. Font sizes and line spacing are given in points.

Before you start

Check these things before you open PTXprint:

  1. You have a Paratext project. PTXprint prints the text of a Paratext project. The project must be on this computer. If you use Send/Receive in Paratext, do a Send/Receive first, so that you have the latest text.
  2. The text has no serious marker errors. PTXprint uses the USFM markers in the text (for example \p for a paragraph or \v for a verse). Run the Basic Checks in Paratext. Marker errors can stop PTXprint or give strange results.
  3. The fonts are installed. Install the fonts that your project needs on this computer. Install them for all users. If a font is installed only for one user, PTXprint may not find it.
  4. You do not have a project, but want to practise? You can still use PTXprint. It can install a sample English Bible (the Berean Standard Bible) for you. See "Get a text to practise with" in the Basic tab chapter.

Open PTXprint

  1. Start PTXprint in the same way as other programs on your computer, for example from the Windows Start menu.
  2. The main PTXprint window opens. It has:
    • tabs across the top (Basic, Layout, Fonts+Script and others). Each tab holds one group of settings;
    • the ☰ button at the top-right, for the main menu;
    • a bar at the bottom with the Save, Print (Make PDF) and Quit buttons.

The first time PTXprint starts, it uses the Default view level. This view shows most tabs and settings. If the window looks too full, you can change to a simpler view: click ☰, point to View Level, and click Basic View or Mini View. Hidden settings still work. See the chapter The main window, menu and view levels.

If PTXprint does not show your projects in the Project list, it may be looking in the wrong folder. See "Use projects from another Paratext folder" in the chapter Help tab and getting support.

Choose the project and the configuration

Everything starts on the Basic tab.

  1. Click the Basic tab.
  2. In the Project list, choose your Paratext project. PTXprint shows the full name of the project next to the list.
  3. In the Layout Configuration area, look at the Name list. The first time, it shows Default.

A configuration is a named set of PTXprint settings for one project: page size, fonts, pictures and so on. Every project has a configuration called Default. You can make more configurations later (see "Keep different settings for different outputs" below). For now, use Default.

Choose the books

On the Basic tab, in the What to Print area:

  1. Click Single Book.
  2. Choose a book from the list. For your first PDF, choose a short book, for example Ruth, Jonah, Philippians or Jude. A short book prints quickly.
  3. To print only some chapters, type the first chapter in From Chapter and the last chapter in To.

Later, to print several books, click Select Multiple Books..., click the books you want, and click OK. See the Basic tab chapter for more ways to choose books and passages.

Make your first PDF

  1. Click Print (Make PDF) at the bottom right of the window (or press Ctrl+P).
  2. PTXprint first saves your settings. Then it makes the PDF. A progress bar shows that it is working. This can take from a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on the number of books and pictures.
  3. When PTXprint has finished, the PDF Preview window opens and shows the PDF.

If a message appears instead of the PDF, read it carefully. Two common messages at the start are:

  • "No books to print" – no book is selected. Choose a book on the Basic tab.
  • "One or more fonts have not been set yet" – go to the Fonts+Script tab and choose a font for the main text (see "Change the main font" below).

Look at the PDF in the preview

The PDF Preview window shows the pages of your PDF.

  • Use the arrow buttons at the top, the Left/Right arrow keys, or the mouse wheel to move from page to page.
  • Use the Zoom box, or hold Ctrl and turn the mouse wheel, to make the page bigger or smaller.
  • Tick Book View (or press Ctrl+B) to see two facing pages side by side, as in a printed book.
  • The title bar shows the name of the PDF file and the time when it was made. Check it, so you know that you are looking at the newest PDF.
  • Click Show main PTXprint settings (or press Alt+S) to go back to the main window.

If you close the Preview window, it is only hidden. It comes back the next time you print. The Preview window can do much more, for example find layout problems and fix them. See the chapter PDF Preview window, layout analysis and page filling.

Change a few common things

After each change, click Print (Make PDF) again to see the result.

Change the page size

  1. Click the Layout tab.
  2. In the Page Setup area, open the Page Size list.
  3. Choose a size, for example 148mm, 210mm (A5). Or type your own size: the width, a comma, then the height, for example 140mm, 216mm.

Ask your printer for the exact page size (the "trim size") before you do a lot of work. If you change the page size later, every line of the book moves.

Change the main font

  1. Click the Fonts+Script tab.
  2. In the Font Configuration area, click the Select Font... button next to Regular.
  3. The Pick a Font (and Typeface) dialog opens. Type part of the font name in the search box, then click the font in the list.
  4. Click OK.

PTXprint then fills in the Bold, Italic and Bold Italic fonts for you from the same font family. If some characters print as empty boxes, the font does not have those characters. See the Fonts+Script tab chapter.

Change the font size

  1. Click the Layout tab.
  2. In the Page Setup area, change Base Font Size (pt). For example, 11 pt is a common size for the main text.

When Lock Ratio is ticked (the normal setting), PTXprint changes the Base Line Spacing (pt) with the font size, so that the page keeps the same look. Headings, footnotes and verse numbers also grow or shrink with the main text. See the Layout tab chapter.

Change between one and two columns

  1. Click the Layout tab.
  2. Tick Two Column Layout for two columns, or untick it for one column.

PTXprint changes the Base Indent for you when you change the number of columns.

Turn pictures on or off

The Pictures tab is not shown in the Mini view. If you cannot see it, click ☰ › View Level › Basic View (or a higher view).

  1. Click the Pictures tab.
  2. On the Global Options sub-tab, tick Include Pictures (illustrations) to print the pictures, or untick it to leave them out.

The first time you turn pictures on, PTXprint needs a list of the pictures (the PicList). It makes this list from the \fig entries in your Paratext text. See "Show the pictures that are in the Paratext text" in the Pictures tab chapter. While you are working on a draft, choose Low Resolution (Smaller File) on the same sub-tab, so that the PDF stays small.

Keep different settings for different outputs

You often need more than one kind of PDF from the same project. For example:

  • a draft for checking, with wide spacing, "DRAFT" on each page and small pictures;
  • a final PDF for the printer, with high-quality pictures and the PDF type that the printer asks for.

Do not change one configuration back and forth. Make a separate configuration for each kind of output. Each configuration remembers its own settings.

Make a new configuration

  1. Click Save at the bottom of the window, so that your latest changes are kept.
  2. On the Basic tab, in the Layout Configuration area, click the Save As button (the icon next to the Name list).
  3. The Save Current Configuration As... dialog opens. Type a name, for example Draft or Final_A5. Use only letters, numbers, brackets ( ), underscores _ and hyphens -. Do not use spaces.
  4. Click OK. PTXprint makes the new configuration as a copy of the current settings, and changes to it.
  5. Now change the settings for this kind of output. The other configuration stays as it was.

Change to another configuration

  1. Click Save first. PTXprint does not save the current configuration when you choose another one.
  2. On the Basic tab, choose the configuration in the Name list.

When a configuration is finished, you can lock it with a password so that nobody changes it by mistake. See "Protect a finished configuration" in the Basic tab chapter.

How PTXprint saves your settings

  • Save (or Ctrl+S) saves the settings of the current configuration.
  • Print (Make PDF) always saves the settings first, then makes the PDF.
  • When you choose a different project, PTXprint saves the current configuration first.
  • When you choose a different configuration, PTXprint does not save first. Click Save before you change.
  • Quit closes PTXprint without saving. Click Save before you click Quit.

PTXprint keeps the configurations inside the Paratext project. So when you use Send/Receive in Paratext, the other people on your team get the same configurations.

Where the PDF is saved

PTXprint saves the PDF inside the Paratext project, in a folder called local\ptxprint. This folder is not shared by Send/Receive. The file name is made from the project code, the configuration name and the books, for example ABC_Default_JHN_ptxp.pdf.

You do not need to remember the folder. To open it, use one of these ways:

  • Click the Open folder containing the PDF button in the bar at the bottom of the main window (Default and Full views).
  • On the Help tab, click the blue link next to Output PDF Location.
  • In the PDF Preview window, click Open folder containing the PDF.

PTXprint makes the PDF again each time you print, with the same name. If you want to keep a PDF (for example the one you sent to a consultant), copy it to another folder, or click Save the PDF with a different name in the PDF Preview window.

When something goes wrong

  • Read the message. PTXprint shows a message in a window, or in the status line above the bottom bar. The message often tells you what to change.
  • Check the view level. If a tab or setting has disappeared, the view level may be too low. Click ☰ › View Level › Full View. You can also type the name of a setting in the Search for settings box at the bottom-left of the window.
  • Check the "Common problems" section of the chapter about the tab you were using.
  • Look in the chapter "Problems and solutions" for problems that are not about one tab.
  • Ask for help. The chapter Help tab and getting support explains how to ask the Support Agent, the PTXprint User Community, or the support team, and how to make an archive file that the support team can use to see your problem.

  • Basic tab and Layout tab – the most important settings for every publication.
  • How do I...? (step-by-step tasks) – short instructions for many common jobs.

The main window, menu and view levels

What this part of PTXprint is for

The main window is where you do all your work in PTXprint. It has three parts:

  • The tabs across the top (Basic, Layout, Fonts+Script, Body and so on). Each tab holds one group of settings.
  • The ☰ main menu button at the top-right corner, next to the tabs. It holds settings about PTXprint itself, not about your book: how to show the PDF, the View Level, the interface Language, and links to Donate and Give Feedback.
  • The bar at the bottom of the window. It holds the Search for settings box, the button to open the output folder, the Quick Run and Layout Only check boxes, and the Save, Print (Make PDF) and Quit buttons.

This chapter also explains three ideas that you need everywhere in PTXprint: configurations, view levels, and how PTXprint saves your settings.

Projects and configurations

A project is a Paratext project – the Scripture text that you want to print. You choose the project on the Basic tab, in the Project list.

A configuration (also called a "layout" or "config") is a named set of PTXprint settings for one project. One project can have many configurations. For example, you can have one configuration called Default for a draft, one called NT_A5 for a small New Testament, and one called Large_Print. Each configuration remembers its own page size, fonts, pictures, styles, front matter and so on.

  • Every project has a configuration called Default. You cannot delete or lock it, but you can reset it.
  • You choose, create, lock, copy and delete configurations on the Basic tab, in the Layout Configuration area. See the chapter about the Basic tab.
  • PTXprint keeps the configurations inside the Paratext project folder. So when you use Send/Receive in Paratext, other people on the team get the same configurations.

How PTXprint saves your settings

  • Click Save (or press Ctrl+S) to save the settings of the current configuration.
  • Click Print (Make PDF) (or press Ctrl+P). PTXprint always saves the settings first, and then makes the PDF.
  • When you choose a different project in the Project list, PTXprint saves the current configuration first.
  • When you choose a different configuration in the Layout Configuration list, PTXprint does not save the current one first. Click Save before you change to another configuration, or your recent changes are lost.
  • Quit closes PTXprint without saving. If you want to keep your changes, click Save or Print (Make PDF) before you click Quit.
  • If a configuration is locked with a password, PTXprint does not save changes to it. You can still change settings on the screen and make a PDF, but the changes are not kept.

Some things are remembered for you (the user) and not for the configuration: the view level, the interface language, the Show PDF choice and the Quick Run setting. These stay the same for all projects and configurations.

View levels

PTXprint has hundreds of settings. Most people need only a few of them. So PTXprint can hide the settings that you do not need. This is the view level. There are four view levels:

View level What you see Good for
Mini Only the Basic, Layout, Fonts+Script and Help tabs, and only the most important settings on them: project, books, configuration name, page size, font size, two columns, the main font. A first look at PTXprint, or a quick draft.
Basic Adds the Body, Notes+Refs, Header+Footer and Pictures tabs, and more settings on each tab (margins, line spacing, bold and italic fonts, the Import Settings button…). Most simple publications.
Default Adds the Diglot, Tabs+Borders, Styles, Advanced, View+Edit, Peripherals, Publications and Finishing tabs, and many more settings on all tabs. Most typesetters. This is the view level that PTXprint uses the first time it starts.
Full Shows every setting, including the Printers tab. Experienced users who need special settings.

How to change the view level: click the ☰ button (top-right), point to View Level, and click Mini View, Basic View, Default View or Full View. The current level is shown in blue and bold in that list. The change happens at once. You do not need to restart PTXprint.

Hidden settings still work. When you change to a lower view level, PTXprint only hides the settings. It does not change them. A hidden setting keeps its value, it is still saved with the configuration, and it still changes the PDF. For example, if you turned on pictures or a diglot in the Default view and then change to the Mini view, the pictures or the diglot will still be in the PDF, even though you cannot see the tab. If the PDF looks different from what you expect, change to the Full view and check the settings again.

Search finds hidden settings. If you use the Search for settings box and choose a setting that is hidden at your view level, PTXprint changes to a higher view level so that it can show you the setting.

Tab labels and highlighted settings

PTXprint uses colour and bold text to help you see what is turned on or changed:

  • The tab that is open now has a light blue background and a bold label.
  • Some tab labels turn blue when their main feature is turned on. For example: Pictures is blue when pictures are included, Diglot is blue when the diglot is turned on, Peripherals is blue when front matter, back matter PDFs or a table of contents is turned on, Finishing is blue when you print more than one page per sheet, and Advanced is blue when one of its special files or options (custom script, changes file, extra TeX or style files, interlinear) is turned on. On Fonts+Script, the word "Fonts" is blue when coloured text is enabled. On Notes+Refs, "Refs" is blue when an extended cross-reference list is used. On Tabs+Borders, "Tabs" or "Borders" is blue when thumb tabs or decorative borders are turned on.
  • Some number settings (mostly on the Layout tab: font size, line spacing, margins, column gutter, header and footer positions and similar) have a label that becomes bold when the value is different from the PTXprint default. This helps you see quickly which values you have changed.

The bottom bar

From left to right, the bar at the bottom of the window has:

  • Search for settings – type a word to find a setting.
  • Open folder containing the PDF – opens the output folder. (Default and Full views.)
  • Quick Run and Layout Only – two check boxes that make printing faster.
  • Print – only appears when you are looking at the secondary text of a diglot.
  • Save, Print (Make PDF) and Quit.

Above the bar, a status line sometimes appears with a message from PTXprint (for example "No books to print"). Click Dismiss to hide it.

When a newer version of PTXprint is available, a Check for updates... button can appear at the top-right, next to the ☰ button. (PTXprint checks at most once a day, only on Windows, and only if Internet use is allowed on the Advanced tab.)

The ☰ main menu

  • Show PDF – choose what happens with the PDF after printing:
    • Preview Pane – PTXprint shows the PDF in its own preview window. This is the usual choice. PTXprint can also use the preview for some editing tools.
    • System Viewer – the PDF opens in the PDF program on your computer.
    • Output Folder – PTXprint opens the folder that holds the PDF.
  • View Level – see "View levels" above.
  • Language – the language of the PTXprint menus and labels.
  • Donate and Give Feedback – open a web page.

Common tasks

See more (or fewer) settings

  1. Click the ☰ button at the top-right of the window.
  2. Point to View Level.
  3. Click Full View to see every setting, or Mini View to see only the most important ones.

Find a setting when you do not know which tab it is on

  1. Click in the Search for settings box at the bottom-left (or press Ctrl+F).
  2. Type a word, for example margin or footnote, and press Enter.
  3. A short list of settings appears above the box. Click the one you want.
  4. PTXprint opens the right tab and highlights the setting. If the setting was hidden, PTXprint changes the view level so you can see it.
  5. To clear the search, click the small clear icon at the right end of the box.

Make a PDF

  1. On the Basic tab, choose the project, the configuration and the books.
  2. Click Print (Make PDF) (or press Ctrl+P).
  3. Wait. A progress bar shows that PTXprint is working. When it is finished, the PDF appears (in the preview pane, the system viewer or the output folder, depending on Show PDF).

Make the PDF faster while you work on the layout

  1. Tick Quick Run (or press Ctrl+Q). PTXprint runs the typesetting only once.
  2. If you only change layout settings (spacing, margins, styles), you can also tick Layout Only (Default and Full views).
  3. When the layout is ready, untick Quick Run and click Print (Make PDF) one more time. This makes sure the table of contents, page references and other details are correct.

Show the PDF in another program

  1. Click ☰ › Show PDF.
  2. Click System Viewer.

Find the PDF file on your computer

  1. Click the Open folder containing the PDF button at the bottom of the window (Default and Full views), or choose ☰ › Show PDF › Output Folder.
  2. The folder opens. The PDF files for this project are in it.

Change the language of PTXprint

  1. Click Save first, so you do not lose changes.
  2. Click ☰ › Language and click a language.
  3. PTXprint closes its window and opens it again in the new language, with the same project and configuration.

Common problems

A tab or setting that I used before has disappeared

Likely cause: The view level is lower than before. What to do: Click ☰ › View Level › Default View or Full View. Or type the name of the setting in Search for settings.

The PDF has pictures (or a diglot, borders, thumb tabs…) but I cannot find the setting

Likely cause: The setting was turned on in a higher view level, and now that tab is hidden. Hidden settings still work. What to do: Change to Full View and turn the feature off on its tab.

I lost my changes after I chose another configuration

Likely cause: PTXprint does not save the current configuration when you choose another one in the Layout Configuration list. What to do: Always click Save (or Print (Make PDF)) before you change to another configuration.

I lost my changes after I clicked Quit

Likely cause: Quit does not save. What to do: Click Save before Quit.

The Print (Make PDF) and Save buttons are greyed out

Likely cause: PTXprint cannot print yet. For example, no project is selected, or another problem is shown in the status line. What to do: Read the message in the status line above the bottom bar. Choose a project on the Basic tab and fix the problem that is described.

PTXprint says "Cannot update PDF file while it is locked!"

Likely cause: The old PDF is still open in another PDF program, so PTXprint cannot replace it. What to do: Close the PDF in the other program and click to try again. To avoid this, use ☰ › Show PDF › Preview Pane.

PTXprint says "No books to print"

Likely cause: No book is selected, or the book list is empty. What to do: On the Basic tab, in What to Print, choose a book or click Select Multiple Books....

PTXprint says "One or more fonts have not been set yet"

What to do: Go to the Fonts+Script tab and choose a font for the main text.

The table of contents or page numbers in the PDF are wrong

Likely cause: Quick Run is ticked, so PTXprint ran the typesetting only once. What to do: Untick Quick Run and print again.

My change to the text in Paratext does not appear in the PDF

Likely cause: In most cases, PTXprint notices that the text changed and processes it again, even when Layout Only is ticked. If it does not, Layout Only may be stopping it. What to do: Untick Layout Only and print again.

The changes I make are not kept

Likely cause: The configuration is locked with a password. A locked configuration is not saved. What to do: On the Basic tab, click the lock button and enter the password to unlock it. Or use Save As to make a new configuration.

Settings reference: The main window, menu and view levels

Every control in this part of PTXprint is listed below, grouped by where it appears.

Main menu (top-right ☰ button)

Show PDF

  • Where: Main menu (top-right ☰ button)
  • Type: Menu button
  • View level: All view levels (Mini, Basic, Default, Full)

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Choose how the PDF is shown after printing: in the preview pane, in your system's PDF viewer, or by opening the output folder.

Explanation:

Opens a small list with three choices: Preview Pane, System Viewer and Output Folder. The choice in blue is the current one. Explanation:

When ticked, PTXprint runs the typesetting only once. Without it, PTXprint runs the typesetting several times (up to 5) so that the table of contents, cross-page details and page layout are correct. Tick it while you are trying out settings. Untick it for the final PDF. PTXprint remembers this setting for you, not for the configuration.

  • Where: Main window
  • Type: Checkbox (ticked by default)

Useful for quick layout tweaks (+1 / −1 spacing or style changes).

PTXprint still re-processes the USFM when the text has changed in Paratext, or when you change a setting that affects the text (the box then shows a dash until the next successful print).

This setting is not saved with the configuration.

Explanation:

When ticked, PTXprint skips the step that prepares the USFM text, and only does the page layout again. This is faster when you only change layout, spacing or style settings. PTXprint still prepares the text again when it is needed, for example when the text in Paratext has changed, or when you change a setting that changes the text (such as which books, footnotes, or verse numbers to include). In that case, the box shows a dash until the next successful print. This setting is not saved with the configuration. If you tick it while the colophon is turned on, PTXprint turns the colophon off. Basic tab

What this tab is for

The Basic tab is the first tab in PTXprint. You come here to:

  • choose the project (the Paratext project with the Scripture text),
  • choose, save, lock, copy or delete a configuration (a named set of settings),
  • choose what to print – one book, part of a book, several books, or a Bible module,
  • check the copyright and license statement for the publication.

Start here every time. Most other settings depend on the project and configuration that you choose on this tab.

Project

Choose your Paratext project in the Project list. PTXprint shows the full name of the project next to the list.

  • When you change to another project, PTXprint first saves the current configuration. Then it opens the configuration that you last used with the new project (or Default).
  • At the end of the Project list there is a blue item, Import.... It opens the Import Scripture... dialog. Use it when you do not have the text as a Paratext project, but you have a Scripture text bundle (a .zip file), or when you want to install the sample text (the Berean Standard Bible).

Copyright & Licensing

(This area is only shown in the Default and Full views.) Click Copyright & Licensing to open the area. It has two parts:

  • Copyright – the copyright statement. PTXprint fills it in from the Paratext project settings. You can change it here. Click Reload copyright from Paratext project to get the Paratext text back.
  • License – choose one of the Creative Commons licenses, All Rights Reserved, or type your own license.

PTXprint puts these texts into the front matter (for example on the title page back) through the variables \zcopyright and \zlicense. Some special codes work in both boxes: (c) becomes ©, (r) becomes ®, (tm) becomes ™, ~ is a non-breaking space, and // forces a new line.

Layout Configuration

A configuration (or layout) is a named set of settings. One project can have many configurations, for example one for a draft and one for the final book. See the chapter about the main window for more about configurations and saving.

  • Name – the list of saved configurations. Choose one to load its settings. You can also type a new name here and click Save to make a new configuration. Use only the letters a–z and A–Z, numbers, brackets ( ), underscores _ and hyphens -. No spaces.
  • The Save As button (an icon next to the name) opens the Save Current Configuration As... dialog, where you type a name for a new configuration.
  • The lock button locks or unlocks the configuration with a password.
  • The Copy configuration to other projects button opens the Copy Configuration To... dialog. (Default and Full views.)
  • Delete removes the selected configuration. For the Default configuration, this button is replaced by Reset.
  • Import Settings... opens the Import Settings dialog, where you can bring settings in from a PDF, a ZIP archive, or another configuration. See the chapter "Importing settings". (Basic, Default and Full views.)
  • Notes – an optional description of the configuration, for you and your team. (Basic, Default and Full views.)

When you choose another configuration in the Name list, PTXprint does not save the current one. Click Save first.

What to Print

Choose one of three ways to say what goes into the PDF:

  • Single Book – choose one book in the list. You can also type chapter numbers in From Chapter and To to print only part of the book. When you choose a new book, PTXprint sets the chapters to the whole book.
  • Portions or Multiple Books – click Select Multiple Books... to choose books by clicking them, or type a list in the box. You can type book codes (MAT MRK LUK JHN), book ranges (MAT-REV) and references (JHN 2:1-12, PSA 23; 100; 117, GEN 1:1-2:3). Use the 3-letter USFM codes (for example JHN, not John). Press Ctrl+B to jump to this box.
  • Bible Module – print a Paratext module (a .sfm file that lists passages to include). Click Choose... to select the module file. Click Edit... to see it on the View+Edit tab. (Bible Module is shown in the Basic, Default and Full views; Edit... in Default and Full.)

If you type in From Chapter or To, PTXprint changes to Single Book. If you type in the book list, PTXprint changes to Portions or Multiple Books.

The FRT (front matter) book is not in the book lists. Set up the front matter on the Peripherals tab instead.

Dialogs on this tab

Save Current Configuration As...

Opens when you click the Save As button. Type a name in Configuration Name and click OK. PTXprint makes a new configuration with a copy of the current settings, saves it, and changes to it. The OK button stays greyed out until the name is valid. PTXprint shows a message below the box if the name has spaces or special characters, or if a configuration with that name already exists.

Tip: Click Save before you use Save As.... Then the new configuration starts from your latest settings.

Lock/Unlock Configuration

Opens when you click the lock button. Locking protects a configuration so that nobody changes or deletes it by mistake.

  • To lock: type a password (up to 16 characters) and click OK. PTXprint saves the configuration and then locks it. The lock icon changes, and dots appear in the box next to the name.
  • To unlock: click the lock button again, type the same password, and click OK. If the password is wrong, nothing happens.
  • While a configuration is locked, Save, Delete and Notes are greyed out, and PTXprint does not save changes (not even when you print). You can still try out settings and print, but the changes are not kept.
  • You cannot lock the Default configuration.

Note: if you click Cancel while the configuration is not locked, PTXprint may still lock it, with an empty password. To unlock it, click the lock button, leave the password box empty and click OK.

Copy Configuration To...

Opens when you click the Copy configuration to other projects button. Use it when several projects need the same layout (for example, a series of New Testaments in related languages).

  1. Click the projects that should receive a copy of the current configuration. The current project is shown in black and cannot be chosen. The Recent list at the bottom shows your selection, and remembers your last 10 selections.
  2. Choose what to do if a target project already has a configuration with the same name:
    • Do NOT Replace Existing Config – skip those projects. Use this the first time you copy.
    • Merge Configurations From Both – combine the two. Settings that were changed in the target project since the first copy are kept.
    • Overwrite With Recent Changes – settings that were changed in this (source) project replace the target settings.
  3. Click OK.

PTXprint copies the saved files of the configuration: the settings, the styles, the changes and TeX files, and the front matter. Adjust lists (paragraph adjustments) are not copied, because they belong to one text. Click Save before you copy, so that the copy has your latest settings.

Select Books To Export to PDF

Opens when you click Select Multiple Books.... Each book in the project is a button. Click a button to select or unselect that book. Hold Shift and click another book to select or unselect all books between the two. The buttons at the side select groups: All Books, Old Testament, New Testament, Deuterocanon, Extra Material, Toggle Books (reverse the selection), and Reset All (unselect all). Click OK. PTXprint puts the books in the normal Bible order in the book list. You can then change the order in the list by typing, if needed.

Import Scripture...

Opens when you choose Import... at the end of the Project list. There are two ways to get a text:

  • Install BSB – installs the Berean Standard Bible, a public-domain English Bible that comes with PTXprint. It is good for practice and as a second text in a diglot.
  • Step 1 – Step 3 – install a Scripture text bundle (.zip):
    1. Download a bundle from the Primary DBL site (Digital Bible Library – you must log in) or the Open.Bible site. Choose a bundle that has the text (not only audio). The USX format is best.
    2. Click Locate... and choose the .zip file.
    3. Check the project name in Assign a Name for the Project and click OK.

PTXprint creates the new project in a folder called _PTXprint inside your Paratext projects folder, and opens it.

Please Confirm...

PTXprint asks you to confirm before something that cannot be undone:

  • "You are about to REMOVE this Configuration" – appears when you click Delete. Click Yes to delete the configuration, or No to keep it.
  • "You are about to CREATE a diglot (or polyglot) configuration" – appears when you turn on a diglot. PTXprint suggests that you first use Save As... to make a new configuration for the diglot.

Common tasks

Start a new publication from an existing configuration

  1. In Project, choose the project.
  2. In Name, choose the configuration that is closest to what you want.
  3. Click Save (so that the latest settings are on disk).
  4. Click the Save As button. Type a new name (for example NT_A5) and click OK.
  5. Now change the settings. The old configuration stays as it was.

Print one book, or part of a book

  1. Click Single Book.
  2. Choose the book in the list.
  3. To print only some chapters, type the first chapter in From Chapter and the last chapter in To.
  4. Click Print (Make PDF).

Print several books, or selected passages

  1. Click Select Multiple Books....
  2. Click the books you want (or click New Testament), then click OK.
  3. Or type in the book list, for example MAT-ACT or PSA 23; 100; 117 LUK 15:11-32.
  4. Click Print (Make PDF).

Protect a finished configuration

  1. Choose the configuration in Name (not Default).
  2. Click the lock button.
  3. Type a password and click OK. Remember the password.

Use the same layout for another project

  1. Click Save.
  2. Click the Copy configuration to other projects button. (Default or Full view.)
  3. Click the target project(s).
  4. Choose Do NOT Replace Existing Config and click OK.
  5. In Project, choose the target project and check the copied configuration.

Set or correct the copyright statement

  1. Change to the Default or Full view if needed.
  2. Click Copyright & Licensing to open it.
  3. Type the copyright text (type (c) for ©), or click Reload copyright from Paratext project.
  4. Choose or type the License.

Get a text to practise with

  1. Open the Project list and choose Import... (the last item).
  2. Click Install BSB.
  3. PTXprint installs and opens the BSB project.

Delete a configuration that you do not need

  1. Choose it in Name.
  2. Click Delete, then Yes.
  3. Before you delete, copy any PDF files that you want to keep to another folder (click the Open folder containing the PDF button at the bottom of the window to find them).

Common problems

My recent changes were lost when I chose another configuration

Cause: Choosing another configuration in the Name list does not save the current one. What to do: Always click Save before you change configurations.

The lock button is greyed out

Cause: The Default configuration cannot be locked. What to do: Use Save As to make a named configuration, then lock that one.

I cannot save, and Delete and Notes are greyed out

Cause: The configuration is locked. What to do: Click the lock button and enter the password, or use Save As to make a new, unlocked copy.

There is a Reset button instead of Delete

Cause: The Default configuration is selected. It cannot be deleted. Reset is shown instead. Be careful: Reset asks no question. It sets all settings back to the PTXprint defaults at once.

The OK button in "Save Current Configuration As..." is greyed out

Cause: The name is empty, has spaces or special characters, or is already used. What to do: Read the message below the box. Use only letters a–z and A–Z, numbers, (, ), _ and -.

PTXprint says "Unknown book code"

Cause: The book list has a word that is not a 3-letter USFM book code (for example John). What to do: Use the codes, for example JHN, MAT, 1CO.

I cannot find the FRT book in the list

Cause: PTXprint does not list FRT as a book. What to do: Set up front matter on the Peripherals tab.

The Primary DBL site and Open.Bible site links do not work

Cause: Disable ALL Internet Use is ticked on the Advanced tab. What to do: Untick it, or download the bundle another way and use Locate....

Copyright & Licensing or Copy configuration are missing, or Reset is greyed out

Cause: They are only available in the Default and Full views. What to do: Click ☰ › View Level › Default View.

Install BSB

  • Where: Import Scripture... (dialog)

Step 3 Assign a Name for the Project

For projects that already have a configuration with this name, settings that were changed in this (source) project replace the values in the target. Use it when this project is the "master" layout for a group of projects.

Layout tab

What this tab is for

The Layout tab sets the shape of every page. Here you choose the page size, the margins (the empty space around the text), one or two columns, the size of the main text and the space between lines.

Come here when you start a new publication, when the printer tells you the page size, or when the text does not fit the number of pages you want. Most settings on this tab change the whole book. After you change them, click Print again to see the new result.

Some words used in this chapter:

  • pt (point) – a small unit used for type. 1 pt is about 0.35 mm. 72 pt is about one inch (25.4 mm).
  • Baseline – the invisible line that the letters sit on.
  • Line spacing – the distance from the baseline of one line to the baseline of the next line.
  • Gutter – an extra empty space. A binding gutter is extra space at the spine of the book. A column gutter is the space between two columns of text.
  • Text area – the part of the page where the main text goes. The margins are outside it.

Page Setup

This area holds the most important settings: Page Size, Base Font Size (pt), Base Line Spacing (pt), Base Indent, the binding gutter and the page-layout options.

Page size

Choose a size from the Page Size list, or type your own. Type the width first, then a comma, then the height, for example 148mm, 210mm. You can use mm, cm or in. Ask your printer for the exact trim size (the size of the finished, cut page) before you start, because changing the page size later moves every line.

Font size and line spacing (and how they work together)

Two numbers control how big the text is and how close the lines are:

  • Base Font Size (pt) is the size of the letters in normal paragraphs. All other text (headings, footnotes, verse numbers and so on) is sized relative to this number. So if you make the base font bigger, the headings and footnotes also grow by the same proportion.
  • Base Line Spacing (pt) is the distance from one line to the next. It is normally bigger than the font size, so that the lines do not touch. For example, 11 pt text with 14 pt line spacing is a common choice.

The Lock Ratio box (ticked by default) joins these two numbers together:

  • When Lock Ratio is ticked and you change the font size, PTXprint changes the line spacing by the same proportion. For example, if you have 11 pt text on 14 pt spacing and you change the font to 12 pt, the line spacing becomes about 15.3 pt. The page keeps the same "look", only bigger.
  • It also works the other way round. If you change the line spacing, PTXprint changes the font size.
  • When Lock Ratio is not ticked, you can change each number on its own. Use this when you want more (or less) space between the lines but the same size letters.
  • When you tick Lock Ratio again, PTXprint remembers the ratio between the two numbers as they are now.

The line spacing decides how many lines fit on a page. PTXprint shows an estimate next to Lines Per Page.

Lines Per Page and the fine-tune buttons

The Lines Per Page number is calculated from the page height, the top and bottom margins and the line spacing. It is updated when you change any of these.

  • If the number is blue, a whole number of lines fits the text area. There is no wasted space.
  • If the number is red, the text area holds a whole number of lines plus a part of a line. That part of a line is empty space at the bottom of each page.

When the number is red, three small "fine-tune" buttons (with an icon of justified lines) become active. One is next to Base Line Spacing (pt). The other two are next to the top and bottom margin settings in the Margins area. Each button makes a small change so that a whole number of lines fits:

  • If more than half a line is spare, the change makes room for one more line.
  • If less than half a line is spare, the change spreads the same number of lines a little further apart (or makes the margin a little larger).

Click only one of the three buttons. Choose the setting you are most willing to change: the line spacing, the top margin, or the bottom margin. The number then turns blue and the buttons become grey again.

Be careful: if Lock Ratio is ticked, the line-spacing fine-tune button also changes the font size a little. If you want to keep the font size exactly, untick Lock Ratio first, or use one of the margin buttons instead.

Binding gutter, Outer Gutter and Mirror Pages

  • Binding Gutter (mm) adds extra space to the inner edge of each page (the edge near the spine). This is added to the Side Margin Width. Thick books need more, because the pages curve into the spine. The gutter changes sides on odd and even pages, so it is always at the spine.
  • Outer Gutter moves that extra space to the outer edge instead. This is used for journaling or wide-margin Bibles, where readers write notes in the outer margin.
  • Mirror Pages makes odd and even pages mirror each other. The header items that are on the left of a right-hand page appear on the right of a left-hand page, so they stay on the outer (or inner) edge. In a diglot (two-language) layout it also keeps the primary text on the inner side, near the spine.

Whether the gutter swaps sides on odd and even pages is controlled by Double Sided Layout, on the Advanced tab, Other tab, in Page Layout and Spacing. It is normally on.

Align Text to Baseline / Variable Line Spacing

This is a switch with Align Text to Baseline on the left and Variable Line Spacing on the right.

  • Align Text to Baseline (the switch to the left, the normal setting) puts every line on a fixed grid. Lines on the front and back of a sheet line up exactly. This is important for thin Bible paper, where the text on the other side can show through. The cost is that some columns may end with an empty line or two. You fix these by hand with the page-filling tools in the PDF Preview.
  • Variable Line Spacing (the switch to the right) lets PTXprint stretch the space between lines a little so that every column is filled to the bottom. This is good for quick drafts and for thicker paper. Front-to-back alignment is lost, and the whole book will re-flow when you change it.

When you switch to Variable Line Spacing, PTXprint also ticks Fill Columns and Allow Unbalanced Columns for you. How much the lines may stretch or shrink is set on the Advanced tab, Other tab, in Page Layout and Spacing.

Notelines (journaling layout)

Notelines prints ruled lines in a wide margin, so readers can write their own notes. When you tick it, PTXprint also ticks Binding Gutter and Outer Gutter, and sets the gutter to 40 mm if it was smaller than 30 mm. A colour button appears so you can choose the colour of the lines. More noteline settings (spacing, offset, type) are on the Advanced tab, Other tab, in Page Layout and Spacing.

Margin Notes

Margin Notes Col Width (mm) creates an extra column at the side of the text. Footnotes, cross-references and (if you choose) section headings can be placed in this column, beside the verse they belong to. Ticking it here only creates the space. To put notes there, choose Side Margin as the position on the Notes+Refs tab. To put headings there, tick In Margin on the Body tab.

These settings are shown in the Default and Full views.

Two Column Layout

Tick Two Column Layout to set the main text in two columns. Untick it for one column. When you change this, PTXprint halves (for two columns) or doubles (for one column) the Base Indent for you, because a narrow column needs a smaller indent.

The settings in the Two Column Layout area only work when there are two columns:

  • Gutter Width (mm) – the space between the two columns. 4 mm is a common value.
  • Vertical Rule in Gutter – draws a thin line down the middle of the gutter.
  • Adjust Top (pt) – moves the top of that line up (negative number) or down (positive number).
  • Thickness of Rule (pt) – how thick the lines are.
  • Allow Unbalanced Columns – lets the two columns on a page end at different heights, by up to a set number of lines.

If you make a diglot (two languages side by side), PTXprint needs the two-column layout, so the Two Column Layout box is greyed out.

Margins

The Margins area sets the empty space around the text, and the position of the header (the line at the top of the page, often with the book name and page number) and the footer (the line at the bottom).

The margin diagram and its colours

Next to the margin settings there is a small picture of a page. It shows one or two columns, the vertical rule, and the horizontal rule under the header, as you have set them. Coloured arrows show what each number measures:

  • Orange – Side Margin Width (mm): from the edge of the page to the text.
  • Red (top) – Start of Page to Top of Text (mm): the top margin.
  • Red (bottom) – Bottom of Text to End of Page (mm): the bottom margin.
  • Purple (top) – Bottom of Header to Top of Text (pt): the gap between the header and the text.
  • Purple (bottom) – Bottom of Text to Top of Footer (pt): the gap between the text and the footer.
  • Green – Space between Rule and Top of Text (pt): the gap between the horizontal rule and the text.
  • Blue – two numbers that PTXprint calculates for you (you cannot type in them): the distance from the top of the page to the header, and from the footer to the bottom of the page.

When you move the mouse over one of the margin boxes, the picture shows only the arrow for that box. This helps you see which space you are changing.

Note that the margins are measured in mm, but the header and footer gaps are measured in pt.

Header and footer position

The header sits inside the top margin, and the footer normally sits inside the bottom margin. So if you make the header gap bigger, the header moves up towards the edge of the page. Watch the blue numbers: if one becomes very small (or negative), the header or footer is too close to the edge of the page and may be cut off when the book is trimmed.

Tick Place Footer Text Above the Bottom Margin if you want the footer inside the text area instead of in the margin.

Tick Horizontal Rule to draw a line under the header. Then use Space between Rule and Top of Text (pt) to set its position.

To see the margins, header and footer areas on the page, tick Guides and Baselines on the Content tab of the PDF Preview window.

Change the Grid Settings dialog (graph paper)

PTXprint can show a "graph paper" grid over the pages in the PDF Preview. This helps you measure things on the page, for example to check a margin or the size of a picture.

To turn it on, open the PDF Preview, go to its Content tab and tick Graph Paper. To change how it looks, click Settings next to it. This opens the Change the Grid Settings dialog. There you can choose:

  • Major Units – centimetres or inches between the thicker (major) lines, plus the colour and thickness of those lines.
  • Minor Divisions – how many thinner lines there are between two major lines, plus their colour and thickness. For centimetres, 2, 5 or 10 work well. For inches, 3, 4, 6 or 12 work well.
  • Place Grid – draw the grid over the Whole Page, only In Margin Areas, or Only in Text Area.

Click OK to apply the settings. The preview is redrawn with the new grid (if Graph Paper is ticked).

Lock UI Layout Settings

When the typesetting is almost finished, you can protect the layout from accidental changes. On the Advanced tab, Main tab, in the General area, tick Lock UI Layout Settings. (This is only shown in the Full view.)

While it is ticked, most of the Layout tab is greyed out (page size, font size, line spacing, columns, gutter, margins and more). The whole Fonts+Script tab and the Styles tab are also greyed out. Untick it to make changes again.

Common tasks

How do I change the page size?

  1. On the Layout tab, in the Page Setup area, click the Page Size list.
  2. Choose a size, for example 148mm, 210mm (A5).
  3. Or type your own size: width, comma, height. For example 140mm, 216mm.
  4. Check the Lines Per Page number. If it is red, use one fine-tune button (see the next task).
  5. Click Print to see the result.

How do I stop wasting space at the bottom of every page?

  1. On the Layout tab, look at the Lines Per Page number. (This is shown in the Default and Full views.)
  2. If it is red, decide which setting you are most willing to change: the line spacing, the top margin or the bottom margin.
  3. Click the fine-tune button next to that setting (next to Base Line Spacing (pt), or in the Margins area next to the top or bottom margin).
  4. The number turns blue.
  5. Click Print.

How do I make the text bigger or smaller without changing the look of the page?

  1. On the Layout tab, make sure Lock Ratio is ticked.
  2. Change Base Font Size (pt). The line spacing changes with it.
  3. If Lines Per Page is red, click one fine-tune button.
  4. Click Print.

How do I put more space between the lines but keep the same letter size?

  1. On the Layout tab, untick Lock Ratio.
  2. Make Base Line Spacing (pt) larger, for example from 14 to 15.
  3. Tick Lock Ratio again if you want the new ratio to be kept.
  4. Click Print.

How do I change between one and two columns?

  1. On the Layout tab, tick or untick Two Column Layout.
  2. If you chose two columns, set Gutter Width (mm) and decide whether you want a Vertical Rule in Gutter.
  3. Check Base Indent. PTXprint changes it automatically, but you may want to adjust it.
  4. Click Print.

How do I add extra space at the spine for binding?

  1. On the Layout tab, in the Page Setup area, tick Binding Gutter (mm).
  2. Type the extra space in the box beside it, for example 5 mm. Ask your printer how much is needed for the thickness of your book.
  3. Leave Outer Gutter unticked.
  4. Click Print.

How do I make a journaling (wide-margin) Bible?

  1. On the Layout tab, tick Notelines. (This is shown in the Default and Full views.)
  2. PTXprint ticks Binding Gutter and Outer Gutter and sets a wide gutter (at least 40 mm).
  3. Change the gutter width if needed, and choose the line colour with the colour button.
  4. Click Print.

How do I put footnotes and cross-references in the side margin?

  1. On the Layout tab, tick Margin Notes Col Width (mm) and type the width of the margin column.
  2. On the Notes+Refs tab, set the position of footnotes and/or cross-references to Side Margin.
  3. If you also want section headings in the margin, tick In Margin on the Body tab.
  4. Click Print.

How do I see a measuring grid on the page?

  1. Click Print so that the PDF Preview opens.
  2. On the Content tab of the preview, tick Graph Paper.
  3. Click Settings next to it to change units, colours and where the grid is drawn.
  4. Click OK.

Common problems

Almost everything on the Layout tab is greyed out

Cause: Lock UI Layout Settings is ticked. This also greys out the whole Fonts+Script tab and the Styles tab.

What to do: Change the view level to Full. On the Advanced tab, Main tab, General area, untick Lock UI Layout Settings.

I changed the font size and the line spacing changed too (or the other way round)

Cause: Lock Ratio is ticked. This is the normal setting.

What to do: Untick Lock Ratio before you change one of the two numbers on its own.

I clicked the line-spacing fine-tune button and my font size changed

Cause: Lock Ratio is ticked, so the font size follows the line spacing.

What to do: Untick Lock Ratio and type your font size again. Then use the fine-tune button again, or use the top or bottom margin fine-tune button instead.

The fine-tune buttons are greyed out

Cause: The Lines Per Page number is already a whole number (blue). There is nothing to fix. The buttons are also greyed out when Lock UI Layout Settings is ticked.

The fine-tune buttons and Lines Per Page are not visible

Cause: They are only shown in the Default and Full views.

What to do: Change the view level from the main menu.

I cannot untick Two Column Layout

Cause: A diglot (two languages) is set up. A diglot needs two columns.

The Base Indent changed by itself

Cause: When you switch between one and two columns, PTXprint halves or doubles the indent.

What to do: Type the indent you want after you change the number of columns.

"Margin Notes on Left/Inner" is greyed out

Cause: It only works with one column. It is also greyed out until Margin Notes Col Width (mm) is ticked.

Margin notes do not appear even though I ticked Margin Notes

Cause: The Layout tab setting only makes the space. You must also send the notes there.

What to do: On the Notes+Refs tab, choose Side Margin for footnotes and/or cross-references.

The header or footer is too close to the edge of the page

Cause: The header gap or footer gap is large compared with the top or bottom margin. The header and footer sit inside the margins.

What to do: Look at the blue numbers in the margin diagram. Make the top (or bottom) margin larger, or make Bottom of Header to Top of Text (pt) (or Bottom of Text to Top of Footer (pt)) smaller.

Columns end at different heights, or there are gaps at the bottom of columns

Cause: With Align Text to Baseline, lines sit on a fixed grid, so some columns can end early.

What to do: For a draft, move the switch to Variable Line Spacing. For a final Bible on thin paper, keep Align Text to Baseline and fix the pages with the page-filling tools in the PDF Preview. In two columns, Allow Unbalanced Columns also lets the columns end at different heights.

The binding gutter is always on the same side of the page

Cause: Double Sided Layout has been turned off on the Advanced tab, Other tab, Page Layout and Spacing. Or Outer Gutter is ticked, which moves the gutter to the outside edge.

The Notelines colour button is missing

Cause: It is only shown when Notelines is ticked.

Settings reference: Layout tab

Every control in this part of PTXprint is listed below, grouped by where it appears.

Change the Grid Settings (dialog)

OK

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog)
  • Type: Button
  • View level: Default and Full views

Explanation:

Closes the dialog and redraws the PDF Preview with the new grid settings (the grid is shown if Graph Paper is ticked).

Cancel

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog)
  • Type: Button
  • View level: Default and Full views

Explanation:

Closes the dialog. The grid in the preview is not redrawn.

Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings

Major Units

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Colour picker
  • Description: Grid: Major line color
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

The color of the major (thicker) grid lines.

Explanation:

Choose the colour of the thicker (major) grid lines. A strong colour (for example red) makes the major lines easy to count. Ignore the tooltip text about Thumb Tabs; it does not apply here.

Minor Divisions

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Colour picker
  • Description: Grid: Minor line color
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

The color of the minor (thinner) grid lines between the major lines.

Explanation:

Choose the colour of the thinner lines between the major lines. A light colour keeps the text readable under the grid. Ignore the tooltip text about Thumb Tabs; it does not apply here.

Major Units

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Grid: Major line thickness
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Values: default 0.2

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Specify the thickness of the major lines.

Explanation:

How thick (in pt) the major grid lines are. Small values such as 0.2 are usually enough.

Minor Divisions

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Grid: Minor line thickness
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Values: default 0.1

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Specify the line thickness of the minor divisions.

Explanation:

How thick (in pt) the minor grid lines are. Keep it at or below the major thickness so the two kinds of line look different.

Minor Divisions

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Grid: Number of minor divisions
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Values: default 12

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Specify the number of minor divisions there should be between the thicker (major) lines. Recommendations: 2, 5, or 10 for centimeters, and 3, 4, 6, or 12 for inches.

Explanation:

How many small squares there are between two major lines. With Centimeters, 5 gives 2 mm squares and 10 gives 1 mm squares. With Inches, 3, 4, 6 or 12 are useful.

Place Grid

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Button
  • Description: Grid: Reload default values
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Clicking this button will refresh the default Grid settings:
Centimeters with 5 divisions (2mm each), red major and light blue minor lines (0.2pt thickness), over the whole page.

Explanation:

Puts the grid settings back to the defaults: centimetres, 5 divisions, the grid over the whole page, red major lines and light blue minor lines, both 0.2 pt thick.

Major Units

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Drop-down list
  • Description: Grid: Select major units
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Choices: Centimeters; Inches

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

The grid can use Centimeters or Inches as the major units.

Explanation:

Choose whether the major lines are 1 cm or 1 inch apart. Use the unit your printer or publisher uses for their measurements.

Place Grid

  • Where: Change the Grid Settings (dialog) › Grid Settings
  • Type: Drop-down list
  • Description: Grid: Starting position (page or margin)
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Choices: Whole Page; In Margin Areas; Only in Text Area

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

The grid can start at the top-left corner of the Page, or at the top-left Margin.

Depending on what you are trying to measure, it can be helpful to position the grid at the top-left corner of the page, or margins.

Explanation:

Choose where the grid is drawn. Whole Page starts at the top-left corner of the page and is best for measuring margins. Only in Text Area starts at the corner of the text and is best for measuring things inside the text, such as pictures. In Margin Areas draws the grid only in the margins, so the text stays clear.

Layout tab › Page Setup

Binding Gutter (mm)

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (not ticked by default)
  • Description: Use binding gutter
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

This is the amount of space to be given on the inner edge of each page for binding (millimeters).

However, if Outer Gutter is enabled this extra space will appear on the outside edge of each page. This can be useful for a journaling layout.

Explanation:

Tick this to add extra space at the spine (inner edge) of every page, on top of the side margin. Thick books need more space because the pages curve into the binding. Ask your printer for a value. Notelines ticks this for you.

Binding gutter amount

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Number box
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views
  • Values: from -200 to 200
  • Only available when: “Binding Gutter (mm)” is selected
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

This amount is added to the ‘Side Margin Width’ amount to the inner edge (or outside edge, if you check ‘Outer Gutter’).

Explanation:

The amount of extra space (mm) for the binding gutter. It is added to Side Margin Width (mm) on the inner edge (or the outer edge if Outer Gutter is ticked). For a normal book, a few mm is common. For a journaling layout, 40 mm or more is common. It is greyed out until Binding Gutter (mm) is ticked.

Base Line Spacing (pt)

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Base line spacing
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views
  • Values: from 4 to 100, default 14
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Base Line spacing in points (pts). Change to increase or decrease space between lines of text.

This is the base line spacing for default paragraph text.

Explanation:

The distance (pt) from one line of normal text to the next. A bigger value gives more space between lines and fewer lines per page. If Lock Ratio is ticked, changing this also changes Base Font Size (pt). Line spacing for other kinds of paragraph (for example footnotes) is set relative to this in the Styles tab.

Page Size

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Drop-down list
  • Description: Page size setting
  • View level: All view levels (Mini, Basic, Default, Full)
  • Choices: 210mm, 297mm (A4); 148mm, 210mm (A5); 105mm, 148mm (A6); 176mm, 250mm (B5); 125mm, 176mm (B6); 210mm, 280mm (PA4); 140mm, 210mm (PA5); 105mm, 140mm (PA6); 8.5in, 11in (Letter); 5.5in, 8.5in (1/2 Letter); 5.25in, 8.25in (133x210mm); 5.8in, 8.7in (147x221mm); 6in, 9in (152x229mm); 184.6mm, 271.6mm (A4 with cropmarks); 165mm, 234mm (KBS max page)
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Type required page width and height,
for example: 148mm, 208mm or select from the list of preset values.

Explanation:

The size of the finished (trimmed) page. Choose a preset or type width, comma, height, for example 148mm, 210mm. You can use mm, cm or in. Get this right before you do detailed page work, because every page will re-flow when it changes.

Base Font Size (pt)

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Base font size
  • View level: All view levels (Mini, Basic, Default, Full)
  • Values: from 2 to 36, default 11
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Set the point size of the main body text.

This is the base font size for default paragraph text. All other font sizes are calculated (according to their factor size) based on this value.

Explanation:

The size (pt) of the letters in normal paragraphs. Headings, footnotes, verse numbers and other text are sized relative to this, so they all grow or shrink together. Typical values are 9–12 pt for Bibles. If Lock Ratio is ticked, changing this also changes Base Line Spacing (pt).

Base Indent

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Number box
  • Description: Base paragraph indent
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Values: default 0.8
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

The amount by which paragraphs should be indented (inches). This also affects poetry indentation. (default=1, min=0, max=4)

The space by which paragraphs should be indented (inches). This also affects poetry indentation. Note that for a single-column text this value needs to be higher than for two-column texts, and the value updates automatically when you change from 1 to 2 columns, and vice versa.

Explanation:

The basic indent for paragraphs and poetry lines. It is measured in inches (so 0.5 is about 13 mm). Each paragraph style uses a multiple of this value. PTXprint halves it when you switch to two columns and doubles it when you switch to one column.

99.9

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Label
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

This is an approximate calculation of the most number of lines that will fit on a page. An exact count is difficult due to ascent and descent values of the main body font.

Explanation:

The estimated number of lines of normal text that fit in the text area. Blue means a whole number of lines fits. Red means part of a line is wasted at the bottom of each page; use one of the fine-tune buttons to fix it. The estimate uses the page height, top and bottom margins, line spacing and the font. It cannot know about headings, pictures or footnotes.

Lines Per Page

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Label
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

This is an approximate calculation of the most number of lines that will fit on a page. An exact count is difficult due to ascent and descent values of the main body font.

Explanation:

The label for the Lines Per Page estimate next to it.

Tweak line spacing (auto adjust)

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Button
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Fine Tune Line Spacing:

This button is only active when PTXprint has a suggestion to shrink or expand the line spacing slightly to minimise wasted vertical space on the page. Click to accept the suggestion.

If there is more than half a line of 'spare' space on the page then the line-spacing will decrease slightly to fit one more line of text on the page.

If there is less than half a line of 'spare' space on the page then the line-spacing will increase slightly to fill the page more evenly (with the same number of lines of text).

If you prefer to keep the exact line spacing specified, then do NOT click this option. Instead, use the similar button to adjust either the Top or Bottom Margin.

Note: if Lock Ratio is ticked, the font size will also change slightly.

Explanation:

Changes Base Line Spacing (pt) slightly so that a whole number of lines fits the page. It is only active when Lines Per Page is red. If Lock Ratio is ticked, the font size changes a little too. If you do not want that, untick Lock Ratio first or use a margin fine-tune button.

Outer Gutter

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (not ticked by default)
  • Description: Place gutter on outer edge of page
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Only available when: “Binding Gutter (mm)” is selected
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

An Outer Gutter can be used to create additional whitespace (for notes etc.) on the OUTER edge of each page as commonly seen in a journaling layout.

Explanation:

Puts the binding-gutter space on the outer edge of each page instead of the spine. Use this for journaling or wide-margin Bibles. You still need a normal side margin for the spine. It is greyed out until Binding Gutter (mm) is ticked.

Lock Ratio

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (ticked by default)
  • Description: Lock ratio of font size to line spacing
  • View level: Default and Full views
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Lock the ratio of the Base Font Size to the Base Line Spacing so that the spacing grows/shrinks according to the size of the font; or the font size changes when the spacing changes.

Explanation:

When ticked, Base Font Size (pt) and Base Line Spacing (pt) keep the same ratio: change one and PTXprint changes the other. When unticked, you can change each one on its own. When you tick it again, the current ratio is the one that is kept. It also affects the line-spacing fine-tune button.

Align Text to Baseline

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Switch
  • Description: Align Text to Baseline Grid (On-Grid/Off-Grid)
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

For high quality typesetting it is best practice to Align the Text to the (baseline) Grid. This ensures consistent line spacing and front-to-back registration.

However, for quick draft printouts or typesetting for thicker paper, Variable Line Spacing mode enables vertical justification which fills each column of text as needed to use up the entire page.

Warning: This is a major 'mode' change. Everything will shift as a result. Consider carefully before changing this setting.

For high quality typesetting it is best practice to Align the Text to the Baseline (i.e. on grid). This ensures consistent line spacing and front-to-back registration.

Note that this may leave larger empty spaces at the end of pages which will need to be manually adjusted using the Adjust List.

Explanation:

This switch chooses between two layout modes. To the left (Align Text to Baseline), every line sits on a fixed grid: best for final Bibles on thin paper. To the right (Variable Line Spacing), the space between lines can stretch so that columns are filled: best for drafts and thick paper. Changing this re-flows the whole book. Switching to the right also ticks Fill Columns and Allow Unbalanced Columns.

Fill Columns

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (not ticked by default)
  • Description: Variable/Increased Line Spacing
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views
  • Only available when: “noGrid” is selected

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

A small increase in the (vertical) line spacing allows the text to stretch to fill the entire column.

This is called vertical justification and is useful for Draft Printouts where the page can be filled without manual intervention to eliminate unwanted gaps at the end of columns. The setting 'Allow Unbalanced Columns' automatically gets enabled when you choose this setting.

Allowing a small increase in the (vertical) line spacing allows the text to stretch vertically to fill the entire column.

This will also enable 'Fill Columns', but you can turn that off to see how much extra space there is at the end of each column.

Warning: This will cause major changes to the layout of the entire document. It will also place headings exactly rather than rounding to the nearest number of lines.

Do NOT use this setting if doing final typesetting for thin Bible paper as front-to-back registration is not enforced with Variable Line Spacing.

Explanation:

Lets PTXprint stretch the line spacing a little so that each column reaches the bottom of the page. It is only available when the switch is on Variable Line Spacing, and it is ticked automatically when you move the switch there. Untick it to see how much empty space would be left at the bottom of each column. The amount of stretch allowed is set on the Advanced tab, Other tab, Page Layout and Spacing.

Notelines

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (not ticked by default)
  • View level: Default and Full views

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Include ruled margins to provide space for personal notes, reflections, and artwork. Typically called 'Journaling Bibles' or 'Wide-Margin Bibles'.

Hint: Set the Binding Gutter to a larger value (>40mm) and enable Outer Gutter. Other settings to control the appearance and spacing of the Notelines are in the 'Page Layout and Spacing' section of the Advanced > Other tab.

Explanation:

Prints ruled lines in a wide margin for readers' notes (a journaling Bible). Ticking it also ticks Binding Gutter and Outer Gutter and sets the gutter to 40 mm if it was less than 30 mm. A colour button appears beside it. More noteline settings are on the Advanced tab, Other tab, Page Layout and Spacing.

Mirror Pages

  • Where: Layout tab › Page Setup
  • Type: Checkbox (ticked by default)
  • Description: Mirror page layout
  • View level: Basic, Default and Full views
  • Greyed out when: “Lock UI Layout Settings” is ticked

Tooltip (the text shown when you hover the mouse over it):

Mirror Pages makes use of an Inner+Outer layout. This will make the left page header the inner header and the right page header will be shown on the outer edge (i.e. headers on odd and even pages are mirrored).

Behaviour for Diglots:
Note that when creating a Diglot, this will place the primary text as the Inner text (closest to the spine), and the secondary text as the Outer text (closest to the edge of the page).

If you always want the Primary text on the left and Secondary text on the right regardless of whether it is an odd or even page, then turn off this option.

Explanation:

Makes left and right pages mirror each other.
