  • Local Front Matter unticks the colophon.

What to do:

  1. Read the status line. PTXprint often tells you what it changed.
  2. Change the setting back if you need to.

I cannot find a setting

A tab or setting that I used before has disappeared

Why this happens: The view level is lower than before. Lower view levels hide many settings.

What to do:

  1. Click ☰ › View Level › Default View or Full View.
  2. Or type the name of the setting in the Search for settings box (bottom-left, or press Ctrl+F). If the setting is hidden, PTXprint changes the view level for you.

The PDF has pictures (or a diglot, borders, thumb tabs …) but I cannot find the setting

Why this happens: The feature was turned on in a higher view level. Hidden settings still work.

What to do:

  1. Change to Full View.
  2. Look for tabs whose names are blue. A blue tab name means a feature on that tab is turned on.
  3. Turn the feature off on that tab.

A setting is greyed out

Why this happens: It needs another setting first, or another setting blocks it. Common examples:

Greyed-out setting What it needs
Almost all of Layout, Fonts+Script and Styles Untick Lock UI Layout Settings (Advanced tab, Full view).
Save, Delete, Notes Unlock the configuration (lock button on the Basic tab).
Two Column Layout Diglot is on. A diglot always uses columns.
Verse (header references) Tick Chapter first.
Pri / Sec (header) Turn on Diglot (or Polyglot).
Parallel Passage Refs Tick Headings on the Body tab.
Hanging Poetry Verse Numbers Untick Marginal Verses.
Between Letters Untick Interlinear on the Advanced tab.
End of Column (notes) Tick Two Column Layout.
Side Margin (notes) Tick Margin Notes Col Width (mm) on the Layout tab.
An Edit... button on the Advanced tab Tick the check box for that file first.
Scale to fit (Finishing) Set Pages Per Spread to 1-up.
Color Hue, Tolerance Choose Print-Spot as PDF Output Format.
Locate... (PDF Preview) Tick Layout Analysis.
Fine-tune buttons (Layout) Lines Per Page is already blue. Nothing to fix.
Mirror (picture) Choose OK to mirror on the picture's Checklist sub-tab.
Generate (Front Matter) Unlock the configuration.
Include Transcelerator Questions The project needs Transcelerator data.

What to do:

  1. Hover the mouse over the greyed-out setting. The tooltip often explains it.
  2. Look at the table above, and see the chapter about that tab.

The Help tab has very few links, or links do not open

Why this happens: Disable ALL Internet Use is ticked on the Advanced tab. PTXprint shows "Internet Access Disabled" when you click a web link.

What to do:

  1. On the Advanced tab, Main sub-tab, General area, untick Disable ALL Internet Use.

PTXprint does not show my projects

Why this happens: The Base Projects Directory points to the wrong folder.

What to do:

  1. On the Help tab, click Change... next to Base Projects Directory.
  2. Choose the folder that contains your Paratext project folders, and click Use Selected.

Getting more help

If your problem is not in this chapter:

  1. Read the Common problems section in the chapter for the tab you are using.
  2. On the Help tab, click Create Report... and read the warnings and errors.
  3. Ask the Support Agent or the PTXprint User Community (links on the Help tab).
  4. Make an archive with Create Archive... (choose only the book that shows the problem), and email it to ptxprint_support@sil.org with a clear description, your PTXprint version and screenshots.

Glossary of terms

How to use this glossary

This glossary explains the technical words and the PTXprint words used in this manual. The terms are in alphabetical order. Where it helps, the definition says which chapter tells you more.

1–9

1-up, 2-up, 4-up, 8-up — How many book pages are printed on one side of a sheet of paper. 1-up is a normal PDF, one page on each PDF page. 2-up puts two pages side by side, for a folded booklet. Set this in Pages Per Spread (see the Finishing tab chapter).

A

Adj List (AdjList, adjustment list) — The list of paragraph adjustments for each book. Each row asks PTXprint to set one paragraph one line shorter or longer, or with slightly narrower or wider letters. You make adjustments in the PDF Preview window, and you can see and edit the list on the View+Edit tab, Adj List sub-tab.

Adjustment (shrink, expand) — A small change to one paragraph so that it uses one line less (shrink) or one line more (expand), or so that its letters are a little narrower or wider. It is used to make pages fill well. See the PDF Preview chapter.

Align Text to Baseline — A layout choice where every line sits on a fixed grid, so the lines on the front and back of a sheet line up. The other choice is Variable Line Spacing. See the Layout tab chapter.

Alpha — How solid a background colour is: 0 is clear (see-through), 1 is fully solid. Used for the background of sidebars on the Styles tab.

Anchor (Anchor Ref) — The place in the text that a picture belongs to, usually a verse, for example MRK 4.39. PTXprint tries to put the picture on the same page as its anchor. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Archive (ZIP archive) — A ZIP file that holds everything needed to make your PDF again on another computer: settings, text, fonts and pictures. Make it with Create Archive... on the Help tab, and send it to the support team when you ask for help.

Auto Page Fill (page filler) — A tool in the PDF Preview window that tries to make every page full, by adjusting paragraphs automatically. It can take a long time. See the PDF Preview chapter.

Auto-update — An option in the PDF Preview window. When it is ticked, PTXprint makes a new PDF by itself a few seconds after you adjust something in the preview.

B

Back matter — The pages after the Scripture text, for example a glossary, maps, an index or a colophon. See the Peripherals tab chapter.

Base Font Size — The size of the letters in normal paragraphs, in points. The size of all other text (headings, notes, verse numbers) is set relative to it. Set it on the Layout tab.

Base Indent — The normal width of a paragraph indent. Other indents on the Styles tab are given as a multiple of it. Set it on the Layout tab.

Base Line Spacing — The normal distance from one line of text to the next, in points. Set it on the Layout tab.

Baseline — The invisible line that the letters sit on.

Bible Module — A Paratext file that lists passages to print together, for example for a lectionary. You can print one from the Basic tab.

Binding gutter — Extra empty space at the inner edge of each page, near the spine, so that the text does not disappear into the binding. See the Layout tab chapter.

Bleed — A picture or colour that goes past the edge of the page, so that no white strip shows if the printer does not cut exactly. Usually about 3 mm. See the Finishing tab chapter.

Book code — The 3-letter code for a book in Paratext and USFM, for example GEN, MAT, JHN or 1CO. Use these codes when you type book lists in PTXprint.

Book View — A way to see two facing pages side by side in the PDF Preview window, as in a printed book.

BSB (Berean Standard Bible) — A free English Bible that PTXprint can install for you, for practice or as a second text in a diglot. See the Basic tab chapter.

C

Caller — The small mark in the text (for example a, b or †) that tells the reader there is a note. The same mark is often repeated at the start of the note. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Caption — The text printed with a picture, usually below it. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Category — A label that groups study notes or sidebars, for example "people" or "places". All sidebars with the same category share one style.

Changes file (changes.txt) — A list of search-and-replace rules that PTXprint applies to a temporary copy of the text before typesetting. The Paratext text is not changed. This is an advanced feature on the Advanced tab.

Chapter label — A word printed before each chapter number instead of a large number alone, for example "Psalm 1". Set it on the Body tab.

Character style (character marker) — A style for a few words inside a paragraph, for example \nd (name of God) or \w (glossary word). Compare paragraph style.

CMYK — The four inks used by most colour printing presses: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and blacK. Many printers ask for a CMYK PDF. Choose it in PDF Output Format on the Finishing tab.

Colophon — A short text at the end of the publication with details about it, for example the copyright, the printer and the picture credits. Turn it on and edit it on the Peripherals tab.

Column Cross-References — Cross-references printed in a narrow column of their own beside the text, as in many reference Bibles. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Column gutter — The empty space between two columns of text. See gutter.

Configuration (config, layout) — A named set of PTXprint settings for one project: page size, fonts, pictures, styles, front matter and so on. One project can have many configurations, for example a draft and a final one. You choose and make configurations on the Basic tab.

Copyright statement — The text that says who owns the rights to the text. PTXprint takes it from Paratext, and you can change it on the Basic tab. It can be printed in the front matter with \zcopyright.

Cover — The outside of the book: front cover, spine and back cover. PTXprint can make cover pages. See the Peripherals tab chapter.

Credit overlay — A small copyright line printed on top of a picture. Some artists require it. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Crop marks (trim marks) — Thin lines outside the corners of each page that show the printer where to cut. Only add them if the printer asks for them. See the Finishing tab chapter.

Cross-reference — A note that lists other places in the Bible about the same thing, for example "Gen 1:1; Ps 33:6". In USFM it is marked with \x. PTXprint can also add cross-references from an external list. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Cutout — A space cut into the side of a paragraph, so that the text flows around a small picture or box. See the Pictures tab chapter.

D

DBL (Digital Bible Library) — An online library of Scripture texts. You can download a text bundle from it and install it in PTXprint (see the Basic tab chapter).

Default configuration — The configuration called Default that every project has. You cannot delete it or lock it, but you can reset it.

Diff PDF — A PDF that shows in colour what changed between a new PDF and an older one. Make it with Compare PDFs on the Finishing tab.

Digit mapping — An option that prints numbers with the digits of another script (for example Arabic-Indic or Devanagari digits) when the text uses 0–9. Set it in the Pick a Font dialog (see the Fonts+Script tab chapter).

Diglot — A publication with two texts side by side on the page, for example two languages. Each text comes from its own Paratext project. See the Diglot tab chapter.

Drop chapter number — A large chapter number at the start of a chapter, two or more lines high, with the text beside it.

Dynamic border — A border that PTXprint draws around text, a heading or a title, and that grows with its contents. Compare PDF border. See the Tabs+Borders tab chapter.

E

em — A unit of width equal to the size of the text. In 10 pt text, 1 em is 10 pt.

End of Ayah — A special character (U+06DD) used in Arabic script to decorate verse numbers. See the Tabs+Borders tab chapter.

Extended note (study note) — A longer note, as in a study Bible. In USFM it is marked with \ef. PTXprint prints extended notes in their own area at the bottom of the page. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

External cross-reference list — A ready-made list of cross-references that comes with PTXprint (or your own list). PTXprint can add these references to the publication. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

F

Fake (faux) bold and italic — Bold or italic letters that PTXprint makes from the regular letters (thicker or slanted), when a font has no real bold or italic typeface.

Fallback font — A second font that PTXprint uses only for characters that the main font does not have. It stops these characters printing as empty boxes. See the Fonts+Script tab chapter.

Final SFM — The text of a book after PTXprint has made all its changes, exactly as it was sent to the typesetter. You can look at it (but not edit it) on the View+Edit tab.

Font — A set of letter shapes, for example Charis SIL or Gentium Plus. A font family usually has four typefaces: Regular, Bold, Italic and Bold Italic.

Font feature — An option built into a font, for example a different shape for one letter, or different digits. Choose features with Select Features... in the Pick a Font dialog.

Footer — The line at the bottom of each page, outside the main text. It can hold a page number, a date or a short text. See the Header+Footer tab chapter.

Footnote — A note that explains something about the text. In USFM it is marked with \f. It is usually printed at the bottom of the page. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Frame size — The width of the area for a picture or box: one column, the full width (span), a page inside the margins, or the whole sheet. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Front matter — The pages before the Scripture text, for example the title page, the copyright page, the table of contents and a preface. In Paratext it is the FRT book. You make and edit it on the Peripherals and View+Edit tabs.

FRT — The book code for front matter. PTXprint does not list it with the other books. Set up the front matter on the Peripherals tab instead.

G

Glossary — A list of words with their meanings, usually at the end of the publication. Its book code is GLO.

Glossary word — A word in the text that has an entry in the glossary. In USFM it is marked with \w ...\w*. Choose how glossary words look on the Body tab.

Glyph — The shape that a font draws for a character.

Glyph collision — Letters or marks that touch or overlap, for example a high mark that hits the line above. Layout Analysis in the PDF Preview window marks these in red.

Graph Paper — A measuring grid that PTXprint can draw over the pages in the PDF Preview window. It is not printed in the PDF.

Graphite — A "smart font" technology from SIL. Some fonts for complex scripts need it. Tick Graphite Rendering in the Pick a Font dialog only for fonts that are made for Graphite.

Grayscale (B/W) — Only black ink, in shades of grey. Choose Print-Gray (B/W) on the Finishing tab for a book printed only in black.

Gutter — An empty space. The column gutter is the space between two columns. The binding gutter is extra space at the spine of the book. See the Layout tab chapter.

H

Hanging indent — A paragraph where the first line starts further left than the other lines. Poetry and lists often use it. Make it with a negative First Line Indent Factor on the Styles tab.

Header (running header) — The line at the top of each page, outside the main text. It often shows the book name, the chapter and verse references, and the page number. See the Header+Footer tab chapter.

Hyphenation — Breaking a long word at the end of a line, usually with a hyphen (-), and continuing it on the next line. PTXprint uses the hyphenation list from Paratext. See the Fonts+Script tab chapter.

I

Image set — A downloadable collection of Bible illustrations. You can search it in the picture catalogue (Show Catalogue... on the Pictures tab).

Imposition — Arranging several book pages on one large sheet of paper, so that after folding and cutting the pages come out in the right order. See Booklet Pagination in the Finishing tab chapter.

Interlinear — Printing a gloss (a short translation) under or above each word of the text, from the Paratext Interlinearizer. See the Advanced tab chapter.

Introduction (book introduction) — The text before chapter 1 of a book, with markers such as \is and \ip. Choose whether to print it on the Body tab.

J

Justification (justified text) — Text where both the left and the right edges of the lines are straight. PTXprint stretches or shrinks the spaces between words to do this. Compare ragged. Set it on the Body tab and the Styles tab.

K

Kashida (tatweel) — A joining stroke (ـ) in Arabic script that makes a word longer. It can be used to make lines look better. See the Fonts+Script tab chapter.

L

Layout Analysis — A check in the PDF Preview window that looks for layout problems (wide spaces, rivers, collisions and missing characters) and marks them in colour on the page.

Layout Only — A check box in the bottom bar. When it is ticked, PTXprint does not process the text again if only layout settings changed, so printing is faster.

Leading — Another word for line spacing: the distance from the baseline of one line to the baseline of the next. PTXprint calls it Line Spacing.

Line spacing — See leading and Base Line Spacing.

Lines Per Page — The number of lines of text that fit on a page, shown on the Layout tab. It is blue when a whole number of lines fits, and red when there is wasted space.

Lock Ratio — A check box on the Layout tab that keeps the font size and the line spacing in the same proportion. When you change one, PTXprint changes the other.

Locked configuration — A configuration that is protected with a password, so that nobody changes or deletes it by mistake. See the Basic tab chapter.

M

Margin — The empty space between the text and the edge of the page. Set the margins on the Layout tab.

Margin notes — Footnotes, cross-references or headings printed in an extra column at the side of the text, beside the verse they belong to. See the Layout tab and Notes+Refs tab chapters.

Marginal verses — Verse numbers printed in a narrow column beside the text instead of inside it. Set them on the Body tab.

Marker (USFM marker) — A short code that starts with a backslash and says what a piece of text is. For example, \p starts a paragraph, \s1 is a section heading, \v is a verse number and \f is a footnote. Each marker has a style on the Styles tab.

Merging mode — How PTXprint lines up the texts of a diglot or polyglot: by chapters and verses, or by a scoring method. See the Diglot tab chapter.

Mirror (picture) — To flip a picture from left to right, as in a mirror. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Mirror Pages — A setting that makes left-hand and right-hand pages mirror each other, so that items stay on the outer (or inner) edge. See the Layout tab and Header+Footer tab chapters.

Monoglot — A publication with only one text (not a diglot or polyglot).

N

Non-breaking space — A space where PTXprint will never break the line. The two words on each side always stay on the same line.

Notelines — Ruled lines printed in a wide margin, so readers can write their own notes. Used for journaling Bibles. See the Layout tab chapter.

O

Odd and even pages — Right-hand pages have odd numbers (1, 3, 5…). Left-hand pages have even numbers (2, 4, 6…).

OpenType — The usual font technology. Most fonts are OpenType fonts. Compare Graphite.

Ornament — A small decorative pattern or graphic. PTXprint can use ornaments in borders and to decorate pages. See the Tabs+Borders tab chapter.

Orphan — In typesetting, the first line of a paragraph left alone at the bottom of a column or page. On the Body tab, Prevent Orphan Words is a different idea: it stops one short word being left alone on the last line of a paragraph. Compare widow.

P

Padding — Empty space inside a box or border, between the edge and the text. Set it in the Border Settings dialog (see the Tabs+Borders tab chapter).

Page filling — Making the text reach the bottom margin on every page, so that no page ends too early. You do it by adjusting paragraphs in the PDF Preview window, by hand or with Auto Page Fill.

Paragraph style (paragraph marker) — A style for a whole paragraph, for example \p (normal paragraph), \q1 (poetry) or \s1 (section heading). Compare character style.

Parallel passage reference — A reference printed under a section heading to show where the same event is told in another book, for example "(Mark 1:1-8)". In USFM it is marked with \r.

Paratext — The program that translation teams use to write and check Scripture. PTXprint prints the text of a Paratext project.

PDF border (Legacy) — A ready-made PDF graphic that PTXprint places behind headings or on every page as a frame. Compare dynamic border.

PDF Preview — The PTXprint window that shows the PDF after you print. You can also use it to fix the layout. See the PDF Preview chapter.

PDF/A — A type of PDF made for keeping documents for a very long time (archiving).

PDF/X — A type of PDF made for printing. PDF/X-1a is the older, strict type (CMYK, no transparency). PDF/X-4 is newer and allows RGB colours and transparency. See the Finishing tab chapter.

Penalty — A number that tells the typesetter how much to avoid something, for example breaking a word. A higher number means "avoid this more". 10000 means "never". Penalties are TeXpert settings on the Advanced tab.

Periph (peripheral section) — A section of the front or back matter, for example the title page or the preface. In the front matter each one starts with a \periph line.

Peripheral book — A book that is not Scripture text, for example front matter (FRT), back matter (BAK), the glossary (GLO) or extra material (XXA, XXB…).

PicList (picture list) — The list of all the pictures in a configuration. Each line gives the picture file, its anchor, caption, size and position. PTXprint makes it from the \fig entries in the text, and then uses only the list. See the Pictures tab chapter.

Placeholder — An empty box printed where a picture would go. It keeps the layout but makes the PDF very small.

Polyglot — A publication with three or more texts side by side. See the Diglot tab chapter.

Primary text — In a diglot or polyglot, the text of the configuration you started from (code L). It controls the page size, margins, headers and footers. Compare secondary text.

Project — A Paratext project: the Scripture text that you want to print, with its settings. Choose it on the Basic tab.

pt (point) — A small unit used for type. 1 pt is about 0.35 mm. 72 pt is about one inch (25.4 mm). Font sizes and line spacing are given in points.

Publication — The book or booklet that you are making. On the Publications tab, a publication is a named set of books that you can print together with others.

Q

Quick Run — A check box in the bottom bar. PTXprint then runs the typesetting only once, which is faster. Untick it for the final PDF, so that page references and the table of contents are correct.

R

Ragged — Text where one edge of the lines is not straight (for example ragged right). Compare justification.

Regular expression — A way to describe patterns of text, used in changes files. This is an advanced feature.

Resolution (picture) — How detailed a picture file is. Low-resolution files are small and good for drafts. High-resolution files are large and needed for printing. Choose on the Pictures tab.

RGB — The colours used by screens: Red, Green and Blue. Compare CMYK.

River — A line of white space that runs down through several lines of text, made by wide spaces between words that happen to be one above the other. Layout Analysis marks rivers in yellow.

Right-to-left (RTL) — Scripts that are written from right to left, for example Arabic and Hebrew. Set the direction on the Fonts+Script tab.

Rule — A thin straight line, for example under the header, between columns, or above the notes.

S

Script — A writing system, for example Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, Myanmar or Han (Chinese). Set the Text Script on the Fonts+Script tab.

Secondary text — In a diglot or polyglot, each text other than the primary text (codes R, A, B…). Each secondary text has its own configuration for its fonts and other text settings.

Section heading — A heading inside a book that names the next part of the text. In USFM it is marked with \s1, \s2 and so on.

Send/Receive — The Paratext command that shares changes with the rest of the team. PTXprint configurations are shared this way. The PDFs are not.

Sidebar — A box of extra text, for example a study note about a place or a person, separate from the Scripture text. In USFM it starts with \esb and ends with \esbe. See the Styles tab chapter.

Signature — A group of sheets that are folded together and sewn or glued into the book as one unit. See the Finishing tab chapter.

Span (Span Width) — The full width of the text area, across both columns. Used for pictures and boxes.

SpeedSlice — A tool in the PDF Preview window that typesets only a few chapters of a long book, so that each print is fast while you fix pages. Always turn it off before the final PDF. See the PDF Preview chapter.

Spot colour — One extra, ready-mixed ink used together with black, for example red for headings. See the Finishing tab chapter.

Spread — Two facing pages of an open book: a left-hand page and the right-hand page beside it.

Strong's numbers — Numbers that identify each Hebrew and Greek word of the Bible. PTXprint can use them in cross-references and to make an index. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Style — The formatting rules for one marker: its font, size, colour, indents, alignment and spacing. Change styles on the Styles tab.

Stylesheet — A list of styles for all the markers. PTXprint combines the Paratext stylesheet with its own additions and your changes. See the Styles tab chapter.

T

Table of contents — A list of the books with their page numbers, usually in the front matter. Turn it on with Table of Contents on the Peripherals tab.

TeXpert settings — About 125 fine settings for the typesetting engine, on the Advanced tab, Other sub-tab. They are for experienced users. Labels turn bold when a value is changed.

Text area — The part of the page where the main text goes. The margins are outside it.

Thumb tab — A coloured block printed at the outer edge of the page, with a short book name in it. When the book is closed, the reader can see the tabs and open the book at the right Bible book. See the Tabs+Borders tab chapter.

Tofu — The empty box (☐) that is printed when the font has no shape for a character. Use a fallback font or another font to fix it.

Transcelerator — A Paratext plugin for making comprehension-checking questions. PTXprint can print the questions. See the Notes+Refs tab chapter.

Trim size — The size of the finished book page after the printer cuts it. In PTXprint this is the Page Size on the Layout tab.

Typeface (face) — One style of a font: Regular, Bold, Italic or Bold Italic.

U

Underfilled page — A page or column where the text stops before the bottom margin. PTXprint lists these in the PDF Preview window, so you can fix them.

Unicode — The international standard that gives a number to every character in every script. A character can be written as U+ and a hexadecimal number, for example U+06DD.

USFM — Unified Standard Format Markers. The way Paratext stores Scripture text, with markers such as \p, \v and \f that say what each piece of text is.

USX — An XML format for Scripture text, used for example in DBL text bundles.

V

Variable — A place-holder in the front matter, written as \zvar|name\*. When you print, PTXprint replaces it with a value from the variables table on the Peripherals tab, for example the title of the book.

Variable Line Spacing — A layout choice where PTXprint may stretch the space between lines a little so that every column is filled to the bottom. Compare Align Text to Baseline.

View level — How many settings PTXprint shows: Mini, Basic, Default or Full. Hidden settings still work. Change it with ☰ › View Level (see the chapter The main window, menu and view levels).

W

Watermark — A light text or picture printed on every page, for example the word "DRAFT". Add it on the Finishing tab.

Widow — In typesetting, the last line of a paragraph left alone at the top of a column or page. On the Body tab, Prevent Verse Widow Words is a different idea: it stops a verse number and a short word being left alone at the end of a line. Compare orphan.

X

XeTeX — The typesetting program that PTXprint uses behind the scenes to place the text on the pages. You never need to use it yourself. Its report of the last print run is on the View+Edit tab (XeTeX Log).

Z

z-codes — Extra codes that start with \z and that PTXprint understands in addition to normal USFM markers, for example \zcopyright, \zvar|...\* or \ztoc|main\*. They are used mostly in the front matter. See the View+Edit tab chapter.

ZIP file — A file that holds other files packed together. PTXprint uses ZIP files for archives, image sets and printer orders.
